Question: A polynomial \(p(x)\) has remainder three when divided by \(x-1\) and remainder five when divided by \(x-3.\) The remainder when \(p(x)\) is divided by \((x-1)(x-3)\) is
Solution:
A remainder must have smaller degree than its divisor. Since \((x-1)(x-3)\) has degree two, write the remainder as \(ux+v\), allowing \(u=0\) if it is constant. Polynomial division gives
\[
p(x)=(x-1)(x-3)q(x)+ux+v
\]
for some polynomial \(q(x)\).

The given linear-divisor remainders imply \(p(1)=3\) and \(p(3)=5\): substituting the root of a linear divisor into the division equation leaves just the remainder. Substituting these same values into our equation makes the product term vanish, giving
\[
u+v=3,\qquad 3u+v=5.
\]
Subtracting the first equation from the second gives \(2u=2\), so \(u=1\), and then \(v=2\). Thus the remainder is uniquely determined as \(\boxed{x+2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
